The Weilüe, a Chinese text composed in the early third century CE, describes the Roman Empire (Da Qin) as a distant kingdom located "west of Anxi (Parthia) and Tiaozhi (Characene and Susiana), and west of the Great Sea," accessible by sea voyage from Parthian territory in a journey that could take anywhere from two months to three years depending on wind conditions. [S1] According to this source, "This country (the Roman Empire) has more than four hundred smaller cities and towns. It extends several thousand li in all directions." [S1] The Chinese account notes that "The king has his capital (that is, the city of Rome) close to the mouth of a river (the Tiber). The outer walls of the city are made of stone." [S1] A later Chinese historical record, the Hou Hanshu, documents that in 166 CE "the king of Da Qin (the Roman Empire), Andun (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus), sent envoys from beyond the frontiers through Rinan (Commandery on the central Vietnamese coast), to offer elephant tusks, rhinoceros horn, and turtle shell," and notes that "This was the very first time there was [direct] communication [between the two countries]." [S3]

results.answer: In the Weilüe's Classical Chinese, Da Qin is described with the following characteristics: "大秦國一號犁靬，在安息、條支西大海之西" [S1], meaning the kingdom is also called Lijian and is located west of Anxi and Tiaozhi, beyond the Great Sea. The text describes the journey to reach it: "從安息界安穀城乘船，直截海西，遇風利二月到，風遲或一歲，無風或三歲" [S1], indicating that from Angu on Parthia's frontier, one travels by boat across the sea, taking two months with favorable winds, a year with slow winds, or three years without wind. Regarding the kingdom's extent and structure, the source states: "國有小城邑合四百餘，東西南北數千里。其王治濱側河海，以石爲城郭" [S1], meaning it has more than four hundred smaller cities and towns, extends several thousand li in all directions, and the king's capital is located near a river with stone walls.
